analysis.one_liner: Bars Wall Street firms and public companies from forcing customers and shareholders into arbitration instead of court.
analysis.headline: The Investor Choice Act, introduced January 31, 2024 with 6 cosponsors, never received a committee hearing or a vote and died in the House Financial Services Committee when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for broker-dealers, investment advisers, and municipal securities dealers to write mandatory arbitration clauses into customer agreements, and would stop them from banning customers from joining class action lawsuits. It would also prohibit public companies from requiring shareholders to arbitrate disputes in their bylaws or shareholder contracts. Investors could still choose arbitration voluntarily, but they could no longer be locked out of court before any dispute arises. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Retail investors with brokerage or investment advisory accounts. Under standard account agreements, most investors today give up the right to sue in court or join a class action before any dispute happens. The bill would let them take disputes over fraud, bad advice, or account mismanagement to court, and would void those clauses in existing agreements going forward.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retail investors in brokerage and advisory accounts

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits broker-dealers, funding portals, municipal securities dealers, and investment advisers from requiring customers to arbitrate future disputes, from restricting which forum a customer can use, or from limiting claims to individual actions or blocking class actions [S2] [S3].

Requires securities exchanges to refuse listing to issuers whose bylaws or shareholder contracts mandate arbitration, and bars registration of any security with such a mandatory arbitration provision [S3].
Voids the banned provisions in agreements entered into before enactment, except for arbitrations already initiated, so existing customer contracts lose their forced-arbitration clauses [S3].
The bill's findings state that mandatory arbitration clauses leverage the industry's advantages to severely restrict the ability of defrauded investors to seek redress [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Broker-dealers, investment advisers, and public companies, which would face lawsuits and class actions in open court rather than private arbitration, along with the litigation costs and public scrutiny that come with it. Firms could pass some of those costs to customers through fees.

drawbacks.text: Industry defenders argue arbitration is faster and cheaper than court for small claims, and that litigation costs would be passed on to customers through higher account fees.
Critics of class actions note that plaintiffs' attorneys often collect most of the recovery, so restoring class suits does not guarantee bigger recoveries for individual investors.
The bill writes its ban directly into federal securities law and overrides the Federal Arbitration Act (title 9), a broad approach that would draw legal challenges and preempts state law choices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary investors, the benefit is real: the right to sue a firm that defrauded you, and to pool small claims into a class action, is the main leverage small account holders have against far larger firms. The costs fall on the financial industry and partly on customers through fees, and arbitration can genuinely be quicker for simple cases. On balance the bill's protections outweigh those costs, but it never got far enough for a committee to test or amend it.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Bill Foster introduced the bill on January 31, 2024 with five Democratic cosponsors: Schakowsky, Casten, Meeks, Velazquez, and Dean [S3] [S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day, and that was the last action recorded for the bill [S1] [S5].
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate companion action appears anywhere in the bill's action history [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broker-dealers, investment advisers, and public companies keep the mandatory arbitration clauses in their customer and shareholder agreements, and defrauded retail investors still cannot sue in court or join class actions. Nobody gained rights the bill would have created, because nothing in it ever became law.

for.name: Bill Foster
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited five Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: Patrick McHenry
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it received no committee action after referral.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the House agenda
against.what_they_did: Brought no securities arbitration legislation to the floor; the bill never received a vote in the full House.

sides.party_line_note: All 7 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican supported the bill and the Republican-led committee never acted on it, though no member ever voted against it on the record.

industries.note: The bill outlaws the mandatory arbitration and class action waivers in their standard customer agreements, exposing them to court suits. Their interest in keeping disputes private and cheap runs directly against customers' right to sue.
The bill bars listing and registration for companies whose bylaws or shareholder contracts mandate arbitration, ending a tool used to keep shareholder disputes out of court.
Exchanges would be required to write and enforce listing rules against mandatory arbitration, a compliance burden, but one that supports retail investor recourse.
Mandated arbitration of investor disputes is a large, steady case stream for providers like the FINRA forum; customers could still choose arbitration voluntarily, but forced filings would end.
